title: Recent theoretical, neural, and clinical advances in sustained attention research
authors: Fortenbaugh, F. C.; DeGutis, J.; Esterman, M.
key_findings: Classic resource-depletion and mindlessness accounts of the vigilance decrement each fail to explain some findings.

Newer resource-control theory: attentional resources stay constant but executive control toward the task weakens and mind wandering takes more resources; opportunity-cost model: effort is reallocated by subjective value, not depleted.
A large reward withheld until the end of a 10-min run eliminated the vigilance decrement in one study.
In a web sample of 10,000+ (Fortenbaugh et al. 2015), sustained attention develops into young adulthood and does not decline until the mid-40s, later than processing speed.
practical_applications: Frame retention as an opportunity-cost decision each moment: give a reason to stay, not a demand to concentrate.
A promised payoff at the end can sustain attention if it is valued and credible.
limitations: Lab vigilance tasks (rare targets on screen), not entertainment video or social feeds.
Review focuses on 2012-2017 literature.

title: Sustained attention across the life span in a sample of 10,000: dissociating ability and strategy
authors: Fortenbaugh, F. C.; DeGutis, J.; Germine, L.; et al.
key_findings: As reported in Fortenbaugh2017: gradCPT web study of 10,430 participants; sustained attention peaks late and age-related declines begin around the mid-40s.
practical_applications: Audiences 45+ may need slightly calmer, clearer pacing; do not assume decline starts at 65.
limitations: Only read via the 2017 review; web-based self-selected sample.

title: Busting the attention span myth
authors: Maybin, S. (BBC World Service, More or Less)
key_findings: The 8-second / goldfish figure appears in a 2015 Microsoft Canada Consumer Insights report but did not come from Microsoft's own research; it cites Statistic Brain.
Sources listed by Statistic Brain (US National Library of Medicine/NCBI, Associated Press) could find no record of research behind the numbers; Statistic Brain did not respond.
Gemma Briggs (Open University): an 'average attention span' is pretty meaningless; attention is task-dependent and shaped by what viewers bring.
Shorter film shot lengths show film-makers got better at grabbing attention, not that attention spans shrank (per the researcher behind that work).
Goldfish are a model system for learning and memory (Felicity Huntingford).
practical_applications: Never cite the 8-second/goldfish statistic; describe swiping as choice, not incapacity.
limitations: Journalism, not peer-reviewed; read via a reproduction in a University of Wisconsin course PDF (bbc.com blocked for fetch).

title: Is Your Attention Span Shorter Than a Goldfish's?
authors: McGinty, J. C. (Wall Street Journal)
key_findings: Popular 8-second claims are not corroborated by science; attention is too complex to reduce to a span of time.
Edward Vogel: measures of college students have been remarkably stable across 20 years; Michael Posner: no real evidence of change since the late 1800s.
The Microsoft report credits Statistic Brain; NLM and AP could not locate the cited numbers.
practical_applications: Use as the citation when correcting the goldfish myth in team briefs.
limitations: Newspaper article; read via reproduction in a University of Wisconsin course PDF.

title: Are attention spans really collapsing? Data shows UK public are worried - but also see benefits from technology
authors: The Policy Institute & Centre for Attention Studies, King's College London (Duffy, B. et al.); fieldwork Savanta ComRes
key_findings: Online survey of 2,093 UK adults, 24-26 Sept 2021.
50% wrongly believe the average adult attention span is eight seconds; only 25% identify it as false.
Researchers: without long-term studies it is impossible to confirm attention spans have declined; Duffy calls the 8-second claim thoroughly debunked.
practical_applications: Expect clients and collaborators to believe the myth; correct it gently with this source.
limitations: UK sample; measures beliefs, not attention.

title: Attention span during lectures: 8 seconds, 10 minutes, or more?
authors: Bradbury, N. A.
key_findings: The widely repeated 10-15 minute lecture attention span ultimately relies on a single key 1978 manuscript and thin evidence.
Treats the 8-second figure as a separate myth from the 2015 Microsoft-commissioned report.
practical_applications: Do not structure content around a fixed 'attention cliff' minute.
limitations: Personal View article in Adv Physiol Educ 40(4):509-513; full text blocked (403), read via search summary/abstract.

title: Everyday attention: variation in mind wandering and memory in a lecture
authors: Risko, E. F.; Anderson, N.; Sarwal, A.; Engelhardt, M.; Kingstone, A.
key_findings: In a video-recorded lecture, reported mind wandering increased with time on task and memory for lecture material decreased; mind wandering related to memory.
practical_applications: Long monotone segments lose viewers gradually; vary and re-hook rather than assume a fixed limit.
limitations: Lab lecture videos; a secondary summary reports other lecture studies did not find increases over time.

title: States of curiosity modulate hippocampus-dependent learning via the dopaminergic circuit
authors: Gruber, M. J.; Gelman, B. D.; Ranganath, C.
key_findings: Better memory for trivia answers people were curious about, and also for unrelated faces shown during high-curiosity anticipation, at immediate and one-day tests.
High curiosity enhanced midbrain and nucleus accumbens activity and hippocampus-reward circuit connectivity.
practical_applications: Place brand/product shots in the waiting period between question and answer, not only at the end.
limitations: Small fMRI sample, trivia and faces not brands; read via abstract/summaries.

title: Interruption, recall and resumption: a meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects
authors: Ghibellini, R.; Meier, B.
key_findings: The Ovsiankina effect (tendency to resume interrupted tasks) appears to be a general tendency; the Zeigarnik effect (better recall of unfinished tasks) lacks universal validity.
Authors suggest conditions that produced Zeigarnik effects (e.g., experimenter authority, involvement) were more common in historical studies.
practical_applications: Treat open loops as curiosity plus urge-to-complete, not as a memory booster; always close the loop.
limitations: Full text not reachable (nature.com redirect, unibe.ch DNS failure); pooled numbers reported by blogs not verified and not used.
license: CC BY 4.0 (Humanities and Social Sciences Communications is open access; not confirmed on page)

title: Absolute coding of stimulus novelty in the human substantia nigra/VTA
authors: Bunzeck, N.; Düzel, E.
key_findings: Two fMRI studies: SN/VTA responses were driven by stimulus novelty rather than rarity, negative emotion or task relevance.
Novelty enhanced learning of familiar items presented in the same context.
practical_applications: Genuinely new visual information (a new angle, a new detail) can recruit reward/learning systems; repetition of the same frame does not.
limitations: Oddball lab paradigm; read via abstract/summary.

title: The effects of edits on arousal, attention, and memory for television messages
authors: Lang, A.; Zhou, S.; Schwartz, N.; Bolls, P. D.; Potter, R. F.
key_findings: Rate of edits (camera changes within the same scene) varied from slow to very fast; as edit rate increased, physiological arousal, self-reported arousal and memory increased.
Authors suggest edits can increase attention and encoding without substantially raising cognitive load.
practical_applications: Change angle/scale of the same product within a scene to hold attention; distinguish from cuts that introduce wholly new information.
limitations: Television era, horizontal screen; read via abstract only; full title may be longer than indexed slug.

title: The limited capacity model of motivated mediated message processing: meta-analytically summarizing two decades of research
authors: Huskey, R.; Wilcox, S.; Clayton, R. B.; Keene, J. R.
key_findings: 142 articles, 683 effects: pooled effect sizes for LC4MP domains (cognitive load, motivation, memory) range r = .314-.398.
Self-report measures give the largest pooled effects, then behavioral, then psychophysiological; no clear evidence of publication bias.
LC4MP: attention to media is governed by viewer goals and involuntary orienting responses to structural features.
practical_applications: Use structural changes (cuts, motion, sound onsets) deliberately to orient attention, while respecting limited capacity.
limitations: Authors acknowledge a 'fruit salad' approach grouping heterogeneous constructs; does not test sub-processes or interactions; only 66 effects had directional information.

title: Attention and the evolution of Hollywood film
authors: Cutting, J. E.; DeLong, J. E.; Nothelfer, C. E.
key_findings: 150 popular films 1935-2005: shot lengths became more correlated with neighbours and their power spectra approached 1/f; authors suggest this may help harness attention.
A 2018 follow-up (295 films 1915-2015) found convergence on 1/f for several dimensions.
practical_applications: Vary shot length in patterns (not uniform rapid cuts) when editing longer story clips.
limitations: Critics (Cinemetrics) note dialogue length drives shot length and the attention link is hypothetical; read via abstract/press/commentary.

title: How video production affects student engagement: an empirical study of MOOC videos
authors: Guo, P. J.; Kim, J.; Rubin, R.
key_findings: 6.9 million video sessions across four edX courses: shorter videos are much more engaging.
Informal talking-head and Khan-style tablet drawings are more engaging; pre-recorded classroom lectures cut into segments engage poorly.
practical_applications: For explainer clips, keep segments short and personal; avoid repurposing long talks unedited.
limitations: Learners in MOOCs, not social-feed viewers; only abstract-level text read, so the length curve was not seen.

title: Counting How the Seconds Count: Understanding Algorithm-User Interplay in TikTok via ML-driven Analysis of Video Content
authors: Masood, M.; Kannan, S.; Liu, Z.; Vasisht, D.; Gupta, I.
key_findings: 68-user lab study plus data donation of 2.65 million videos.
Users spend most time on a few topics but topics change often; feeds individualise rather than converge to trending.
Recommendations do not reflect just-performed actions (contrary to folk theory).
Users like topic change: session novelty relates to perceived content quality; sequence of videos matters.
Content features predict watching >10% of a video with ~70% accuracy, leaving much behaviour unexplained.
practical_applications: Do not over-trust folk theories about 'the algorithm'; vary topics across a posting series; content quality explains only part of retention.
limitations: Participants mostly 18-34, browsing TikTok on macOS web browser, not the mobile app; VLM clustering choices.

title: Measure key moments for audience retention (YouTube Help)
authors: YouTube / Google
key_findings: Flat line = viewers watch that part start to finish; gradual decline is typical; spikes = rewatching/sharing (strong or confusing content); dips = leaving/skipping.
Intro metric = share of audience still watching after the first 30 seconds; align opening with title and thumbnail.
Typical retention compares a video with the channel's 10 latest videos of similar length; move compelling content earlier.
practical_applications: Read post-publication graphs against the RETENTION_REVIEW table; benchmark against own videos, not internet averages.
limitations: Platform documentation; no published methodology or effect sizes.

title: Creative best practices for performance ads (TikTok Business Help Center)
authors: TikTok for Business
key_findings: Prioritise the hook in the first 6 seconds; introduce the content proposition in the first 3 seconds.
Use sound/music; captions or text overlays at 5-10 words per second; 9:16 vertical, 720p+, inside UI safe zone.
Feature creators, employees or customers; end with a clear CTA; structure hook -> USPs -> CTA; refresh creatives when performance declines.
practical_applications: Use as craft defaults for product clips, labelled as platform guidance.
limitations: No studies or data cited on the page; written for paid performance ads.

title: Best practices for Instagram video ads (Meta Business Help Center)
authors: Meta
key_findings: Feature brand and key message within the first 3 seconds; 6-15 second videos are more effective in feed and stories; hook with motion or a compelling first frame.
Design for sound-off with subtitles and supers, but music/voiceover helps those who listen; Meta reports feed video ads have 2.25x higher CTA CTR when watched with sound on.
Provide key info early because many people interact before the video ends; native, non-ad-like creative performs better; test and iterate.
practical_applications: Brand and frame visible in first seconds; every clip must work muted and unmuted.
limitations: Platform guidance without methodology; retrieved through Meta's official help-article tool.

title: Optimize your ad creative for Instagram (Meta Business Help Center)
authors: Meta
key_findings: Showcase brand/product within the first 3 seconds; under 15 s in feed, under 10 s in stories.
Structured storytelling (problem > solution > result, transformation, day in the life) and product demos help performance.
Product-focused creative for lower-funnel results, people-focused creative for brand objectives; aim for frequency of 2-3 impressions per person per 7 days.
practical_applications: Choose product-focused vs people-focused clips by campaign goal; watch frequency to avoid fatigue.
limitations: Platform guidance, no methodology.

title: Generational differences in work-related attitudes: a meta-analysis
authors: Costanza, D. P.; et al.
key_findings: 20 studies, 18 pairwise comparisons, 19,961 subjects across Traditionals, Boomers, Gen X and Millennials.
Relationships between generation and work outcomes are moderate to small, essentially zero in many cases; meaningful differences probably do not exist on the variables examined.
A 2024 meta-analytic review (Ravid, Costanza, Romero, J Organ Behav) reportedly found few systematic meaningful differences.
practical_applications: Brief by life situation and age-related needs, not by generation label.
limitations: Work attitudes, not media habits; Gen Z not included; read via abstract/search summary.

title: Are Generational Categories Meaningful Distinctions for Workforce Management?
authors: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
key_findings: Committee charged to assess whether generational categories are meaningful for workforce management; notes advice on managing generations is prevalent but sometimes contradictory.
practical_applications: Cite as an authoritative caution against generation-based targeting.
limitations: Only front matter read; conclusions not read this session.

title: How Pew Research Center will report on generations moving forward
authors: Pew Research Center (Parker, K.)
key_findings: Generational analysis only when historical data allow comparing groups at the same life stage; age, period and cohort effects are hard to separate.
Demographic shifts can look like generational differences; great diversity within generations.
Labels like Gen Z/Millennial are reference points, not scientific facts; used sparingly to avoid reinforcing stereotypes.
practical_applications: Remove generation stereotypes from briefs; use age/life-stage and context.
limitations: Methodological statement, US focus.

title: How to design font size for older adults: a systematic literature review with a mobile device
authors: Hou, G.; Anicetus, U.; He, J.
key_findings: 12 studies: older adults prefer larger fonts, but there is a critical size beyond which readability declines ('bigger may not always mean better').
Reading speed declines sharply below roughly 9-18 arcmin and declines less steeply above roughly 60-180 arcmin.
Recommended sizes range ~8-22 pt across devices, languages and tasks; higher contrast and more line spacing help; inconsistent units across studies, arcmin proposed.
practical_applications: Subtitles for 45+ viewers: large, high-contrast, generous line spacing, but not so large that lines break every two words.
limitations: Mixed devices and languages (Chinese, Japanese, English); no Thai script; small study count.
license: CC BY (Frontiers; not confirmed on fetched portion)

title: Older Users and Web Accessibility: Meeting the Needs of Ageing Web Users
authors: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI)
key_findings: Age-related impairments overlap with disabilities: reduced contrast sensitivity, colour perception and near focus; hearing loss for higher pitches and separating overlapping sounds (e.g., audio with background music); reduced short-term memory and easier distraction.
WCAG guidance for people with disabilities also serves older users.
practical_applications: Duck music under voiceover; high-contrast captions; simple, low-distraction layouts for presbyopia content.
limitations: Web-focused overview, not video-specific research.

title: The recognition of time-compressed speech as a function of age in listeners with cochlear implants or normal hearing
authors: Tinnemore, A. R.; Montero, L.; Gordon-Salant, S.; Goupell, M. J.
key_findings: Normal-hearing younger, middle-aged and older listeners performed similarly at normal rate; age-by-compression interactions were not significant at 20% but significant at 40% and 60% compression.
Middle-aged (52-64) and older groups did not differ at 40-60% compression, suggesting age effects begin before 65.
Processing-speed test (Symbol Search) did not predict performance.
practical_applications: Do not speed up TTS to fit a duration in content for 45+ customers; cut the script instead.
limitations: English sentences, artificial time compression (natural fast speech may be harder per other work); first ~100k characters read.
license: CC BY (Frontiers; not confirmed on fetched portion)

title: ISO 24495-1:2023 Plain language - Part 1: Governing principles and guidelines
authors: ISO/TC 37
key_findings: Four principles: relevant, findable, understandable, usable; identify readers and purpose; evaluate with readers.
Applies to printed/digital text, may help video creators; does not cover accessibility (points to WCAG and EN 301 549).
practical_applications: English clips for tourists: short plain sentences, numbers clear, visuals carry the story.
limitations: Paid standard; only publisher page and catalogue summaries read.
